domains.name: Quantum Computing: Qubits, Algorithms & the Cryptographic Future
domains.summary: From the qubit to the verdict: superposition and interference, the landmark algorithms, the hardware reality, post-quantum cryptography, and an honest grading of the hype — 46 years from suggestion to standards.

scenarios.title: All Answers at Once?
scenarios.situation: A startup pitch claims their quantum processor 'tries all answers at once, so it solves every problem instantly.' An investor asks you to sanity-check the claim before a term sheet.
scenarios.prompt: What is the technically honest correction?
choices: Misleading: a superposition holds many computational paths, but measurement reveals only one sample from a probability distribution. Without interference choreography amplifying the right answer, parallelism buys nothing — which is why quantum speedups are rare and problem-specific, not general.
Correct — superposition means every problem is solved in parallel instantly.
Correct for search problems, wrong for everything else.
Wrong — quantum computers are slower than classical ones at everything.
scenarios.why: The Born rule is the whole story: measuring |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ returns 0 with probability |α|² and 1 with probability |β|², collapsing the state. You can compute on all possibilities in superposition, but reading the answer out reveals one sample. Every real algorithm — Deutsch-Jozsa, Grover, Shor — is an interference pattern designed by hand: amplitudes for wrong answers cancel, the right answer reinforces, and then the measurement pays out.
scenarios.hint: If the machine 'tried everything,' how would you read the answer back out?

scenarios.title: Vector, Not Switch
scenarios.situation: A junior engineer describes a qubit as 'a bit that is 0 and 1 at the same time.' She's about to design a quantum circuit simulator based on that mental model.
choices: A qubit's state is |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ with |α|² + |β|² = 1 — a precise geometric statement: the qubit points somewhere on the Bloch sphere. Every single-qubit operation is a rotation of that arrow. The '0 and 1 at once' slogan is not a useful engineering model.
The slogan is fine; simulators don't need the geometry.
A qubit is exactly a probabilistic classical bit.
A qubit is a bit with three values: 0, 1, and both.
scenarios.why: The Bloch sphere is the working model: north pole |0⟩, south pole |1⟩, and every other point a distinct superposition with definite complex amplitudes. Gates are rotations. This precision matters — interference, the real trick of quantum algorithms, is choreography of those amplitudes, and you cannot choreograph what you model as a slogan.
scenarios.hint: What does a Hadamard gate do to the arrow?

scenarios.title: Shor vs. Your Passwords
scenarios.situation: After reading about Shor's algorithm (1994), a client's CISO asks: 'Does this mean all our encryption is already broken? Should we re-encrypt everything with AES-256 today?'
choices: No — and AES isn't the problem. Shor breaks RSA/ECC in principle, but only on a fault-tolerant machine that does not exist. Symmetric encryption (AES) and hashing are only quadratically weakened by Grover's algorithm. The honest statement: public-key cryptography has a known expiration date — which is why NIST finalized post-quantum standards (FIPS 203/204/205) on August 13, 2024, and the migration of public-key infrastructure is the real work.
Yes — Shor breaks all encryption, so re-encrypt everything immediately.
Yes for RSA, and AES-256 is also fully broken by Grover's algorithm.
No — quantum computers will never threaten any encryption.
scenarios.why: Scope the threat precisely: Shor's polynomial-time factoring and discrete-log algorithm targets public-key systems (RSA, ECC); Grover gives only a quadratic speedup against symmetric crypto, which larger key sizes absorb. The 46-year arc from Feynman's 1980 suggestion to the 2024 NIST standards is the story of a threat seen coming decades out — the migration, not panic, is the response.
scenarios.hint: Which of the client's systems use public-key crypto, and which use symmetric?

scenarios.title: The Qubit Count Press Release
scenarios.situation: A hardware vendor announces a 2,000-qubit processor and claims to be '2,000 times closer to breaking RSA than last year's 1,000-qubit machine.'
scenarios.prompt: How do you grade the claim?
choices: Misleading. A thousand noisy physical qubits are not one-thousandth of the way to a cryptographically relevant machine — without error correction, qubit count alone says almost nothing about capability. Logical (error-corrected) qubits are the metric that matters, and the industry still counts those in single digits.
Accurate — qubit count is the standard progress metric.
Accurate, but only for superconducting qubits, not trapped ions.
Wrong direction — more qubits make RSA harder to break.
scenarios.why: Decoherence is why the machines are hard: a qubit stays quantum only while isolated, and heat, stray fields, even control wiring collapse superpositions toward classical noise. Error correction protects quantum information without ever reading it (no-cloning forbids copying it out to check). Until logical qubits scale, physical qubit counts are a press-release metric, not a capability metric.
scenarios.hint: How many of those 2,000 qubits are logical — error-corrected — qubits?

scenarios.title: Judging a 'Quantum Advantage' Claim
scenarios.situation: A lab press release claims 'quantum advantage' on an optimization problem: their 80-qubit device beat the best classical result — but the classical baseline is from 2019, the problem instance was chosen by the hardware team, and no independent group has reproduced it.
scenarios.prompt: You are asked to grade the claim, capstone-style.
choices: Contested at best. The checklist: is the classical baseline current (remember how improved classical simulations narrowed Google's 2019 Sycamore 'supremacy' claim on random-circuit sampling — a benchmark with no practical use)? Was the problem chosen neutrally? Is it reproduced independently? Does the task have practical use? Supremacy on a useless or cherry-picked task is a physics milestone, not a product — and certainly not a verdict.
Accept it — 80 qubits beating classical is advantage by definition.
Reject it — quantum advantage is impossible in principle.
Accept it, but only if the lab publishes the circuit depth.
scenarios.why: This is the capstone skill: grade hype with a fixed rubric. Google's 2019 Sycamore result demonstrated a task hard for classical supercomputers at the time — and subsequent classical improvements narrowed the gap. The pattern repeats: baseline freshness, problem selection, independent reproduction, and practical utility are the four questions, asked in that order, every time.
scenarios.hint: What would change your grade — in either direction?

scenarios.title: You Cannot Copy the Qubit
scenarios.situation: An engineer proposes debugging a quantum program the classical way: copy the qubit register mid-computation, inspect the copy, and continue. Another proposes backing up quantum state to disk 'just in case.'
choices: The no-cloning theorem (proved 1982): no operation copies an unknown quantum state |ψ⟩ into |ψ⟩|ψ⟩. It's a theorem, not a hardware limitation — no variables can be copied, no state inspected mid-computation, and error correction must protect quantum information without ever reading it. It is also the bedrock of quantum cryptography: eavesdropping disturbs the state and reveals itself.
They fail only on current hardware; future machines will allow copying.
Copying works but is too slow to be useful for debugging.
The proposals are fine — the theorem only applies to entangled states.
scenarios.why: No-cloning is what makes quantum computing feel alien and what makes quantum key distribution possible: any attempt to read an unknown state disturbs it. Debugging therefore means reasoning about circuits and statistics of measurement outcomes — never peeking at the state itself. Design your tools around the theorem, not against it.
scenarios.hint: If you can't copy the state, what *can* you log?

lessons.title: Quantum Computing: Qubits, Algorithms & the Cryptographic Future — Core concepts
concepts: The qubit is a vector, not a switch: |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ with |α|² + |β|² = 1 — a point on the Bloch sphere, and every single-qubit gate a rotation of that arrow.

The Born rule: measurement returns 0 with probability |α|² and 1 with probability |β|², collapsing the state. A million measurements reveal the probabilities, never the amplitudes — which is why 'trying all answers at once' buys nothing by itself.
n qubits hold one vector in a 2ⁿ-dimensional space. That exponential dimension is the entire reason quantum computing is interesting — and the entire reason it is hard to simulate classically.

Interference is the real trick: quantum algorithms arrange amplitudes so wrong answers cancel and the right answer reinforces. Deutsch-Jozsa, Grover, and Shor are interference patterns designed by hand.
No-cloning (theorem, 1982): an unknown quantum state cannot be copied. No mid-computation inspection, no backups — and the bedrock of quantum cryptography.

Decoherence: qubits stay quantum only while isolated. The hardware war is fought against heat, stray fields, and control wiring — which is why logical (error-corrected) qubits, still counted in single digits, are the metric that matters.

The 46-year arc: 1980 (Benioff/Feynman) → 1985 (Deutsch) → 1994 (Shor) → 1996 (Grover) → 2019 (Sycamore) → 2022 (Nobel for entanglement experiments) → August 13, 2024 (NIST finalizes FIPS 203/204/205 post-quantum standards) → 2026: no fault-tolerant machine exists.

example.code:
pip install qiskit qiskit-aer
python3 - <<'EOF'
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit_aer import AerSimulator
qc = QuantumCircuit(2, 2)
qc.h(0)          # superposition on qubit 0
qc.cx(0, 1)      # entangle: Bell pair
qc.measure([0,1],[0,1])
counts = AerSimulator().run(qc, shots=1000).result().get_counts()
print(counts)    # ~{'00': 500, '11': 500}: correlated, never 01/10
EOF
example.walkthrough: Build a Bell pair: Hadamard puts qubit 0 in superposition, CNOT entangles it with qubit 1. The measurement statistics show perfect correlation — 00 or 11, never mixed — the signature of entanglement that no classical description reproduces. This is the open-source lab (Qiskit) the track's Module 9 walks through.

pitfalls: Common trap: 'superposition = trying everything at once.' Measurement yields one sample; only interference choreography extracts an answer.
Common trap: 'more physical qubits = closer to breaking RSA.' Without error correction, qubit count says almost nothing; count logical qubits.
Common trap: 'Shor means all encryption is broken.' It targets public-key crypto on a machine that doesn't exist; symmetric crypto is only quadratically weakened.
Common trap: 'quantum computers will replace classical ones.' They accelerate specific structured problems and remain coprocessors for the foreseeable future.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab: build the Bell-pair circuit in Qiskit, then grade a real 'quantum advantage' press release against the four-question rubric.

labs.title: Open-source lab: your first entangled circuit in Qiskit
labs.objective: Install Qiskit, build a Bell-pair circuit, simulate 1000 shots, and interpret the correlated statistics.
steps: Install qiskit and qiskit-aer in a fresh virtual environment.
Write bell.py: 2 qubits, Hadamard on qubit 0, CNOT 0→1, measure both.
Run the Aer simulator for 1000 shots and print the counts dictionary.
Verify the signature of entanglement: only '00' and '11' appear, roughly 500 each, never '01' or '10'.
Add a one-paragraph note to the file explaining, in your own words, why this correlation has no classical explanation.

checks.hint: Run bell.py and look for the '00'/'11' counts in the output.

labs.title: Capstone: grade a quantum-advantage claim
labs.objective: Apply the four-question hype rubric to a real press release and write a graded verdict.
steps: Find a recent 'quantum advantage/supremacy' press release or paper announcement.

Create ~/quantum/claim-grade.md with the four questions: (1) Is the classical baseline current? (2) Was the problem chosen neutrally? (3) Has it been independently reproduced? (4) Does the task have practical use?
Answer each question with evidence quoted or cited from the announcement.
Write your verdict: accepted / contested / rejected — with the one fact that would change your grade.
Print the file to confirm the verdict and the grade-changing fact are present.

checks.hint: cat your claim-grade.md and confirm the verdict line exists.
Confirm all four rubric questions are answered (grep for 'baseline').

cheatsheet: |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩, |α|² + |β|² = 1. Qubit = point on Bloch sphere; gates = rotations.
Born rule: measurement pays out probabilities |α|²/|β|² and collapses the state.
n qubits = one vector in 2ⁿ dimensions. Entanglement = joint states that don't factor.
Interference is the trick: wrong answers cancel, right answer reinforces.
No-cloning (1982): unknown states can't be copied — no peeking, bedrock of quantum crypto.
Decoherence: isolation is everything. Count logical qubits, not physical ones.
Shor → public-key expiry (fault-tolerant machine needed). Grover → quadratic hit on symmetric only.
1980 suggestion → 2024 NIST FIPS 203/204/205 standards. 2026: no fault-tolerant machine exists.

glossary.def: The quantum unit of information: a normalized vector α|0⟩ + β|1⟩, visualized on the Bloch sphere.
A qubit state combining basis states with complex amplitudes; measurement collapses it per the Born rule.
Joint multi-qubit states that cannot be described as independent single-qubit states.
Amplitude cancellation/reinforcement arranged by quantum algorithms to amplify correct answers.
Loss of quantum behavior through interaction with the environment.
An error-corrected qubit built from many physical qubits; the capability metric that matters.
Classical algorithms believed resistant to quantum attack; NIST standardized ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA in 2024.

checklist: I can write the qubit state equation and explain the Bloch sphere.
I can state the Born rule and why 'try all answers at once' is misleading.
I can explain interference as the mechanism behind Deutsch-Jozsa, Grover, and Shor.
I scope Shor's threat correctly: public-key, fault-tolerant machine, not yet real.
I grade advantage claims with the four-question rubric.

chat.persona: A quantum-skeptical physicist-tutor: precise with the math, ruthless with hype, always asking for the classical baseline.
